Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette:
Amir's Case

Amir was thirty-seven when the stalking began, a firefighter with twelve years on the job and a marriage that had weathered its share of strain. In the spring of two years ago, a woman he had met briefly at a community event became convinced they had a connection. What began as messages escalated to appearances—outside the firehouse, near his home, at the grocery store where his wife shopped. She knew details about his schedule, his routes, the places he frequented. For months, Amir tried to be reasonable, to de-escalate, to assume there was some misunderstanding that could be clarified. But the woman's obsession deepened. She followed him on his bicycle during his commute to the station, maintaining a distance but close enough that he could hear her breathing, the scrape of her shoes on the pavement. She waited in the parking lot at dawn. She called his home phone at three in the morning. The police became involved. A restraining order was filed. And then, one evening in August, she appeared at the back door of his house while his wife was upstairs. When Amir opened it, she was holding a knife.

The police arrested her before anyone was hurt, but something in Amir fractured that night in a way the physical world could not repair. In the weeks that followed, he returned to work, but he was not the same man who had left. His colleagues noticed it immediately—the way he positioned himself in the station so his back was never to a door, the way he flinched at sounds that would have barely registered before. When an alarm sounded unexpectedly during a drill, Amir's heart would hammer so violently he thought it might tear through his ribs. He had come to believe that his hypervigilance was not a symptom but a necessity, that any moment of relaxation might be the one that cost him his life. The woman was in custody, the restraining order ironclad, but Amir was certain that none of this mattered—that danger was still coming, that he had simply not seen it arrive yet.

The bicycle became unbearable. During his commute, every sound behind him—a car door, a voice, the whistle of wind—sent him into a spiral of scanning and checking. He would pull over, turn around, convince himself that someone was tracking him. After three weeks, he stopped cycling altogether and drove instead, though the car felt like a cage and the traffic lights like traps where he could be cornered. When he entered the firehouse now, his eyes immediately found the exits, catalogued them, measured distances. He watched his colleagues in a way that made them uncomfortable, searching their faces and body language for signs of threat that he could not articulate but felt with absolute certainty. The memory itself was fragmented and overwhelming—not a coherent narrative but a flood of sensation and dread that would arrive without warning, triggered by something as small as a woman's voice in the grocery store or the sight of someone on a bicycle. When it came, Amir would have to leave, to find a bathroom or a quiet corner, because the emotion was so total, so consuming, that he could not speak or function. He knew what had happened, but the words would not come; he could only feel the terror and the shame of feeling it.

What frightened Amir most was what this fear said about him. He had always understood himself as capable, as someone who ran into burning buildings while others ran out. Now he was a man who scanned exits and watched strangers and could not ride a bicycle without terror. He had come to believe that he had permanently changed for the worse, that something fundamental in him had broken and could not be repaired. The hypervigilance, the way he monitored every sound and every face, felt like evidence that he was losing his mind—that his reactions had become so disproportionate to the actual threat that he was, in fact, going crazy. These convictions fed back into his vigilance; because he believed himself weak and damaged, every moment of alertness felt necessary, every scan of a room justified. The more he watched for danger, the more danger he seemed to find, and the more convinced he became that he was unraveling. His wife had begun to sleep in the guest room. His captain had quietly suggested that he consider leave. It was only when a colleague finally confronted him directly—asking if he had talked to anyone about what happened—that Amir recognized he could no longer manage this alone. He came to his first session pale and exhausted, describing himself as broken, afraid that therapy itself might confirm what he already believed: that the man he had been was gone, and that the frightened, hypervigilant stranger wearing his skin was all that remained.
